idiom_name: interface with a default implementation, implemented with `by` delegation to the twin object
implementation_notes: Kotlin classes have one superclass, but interfaces may carry implementations (they still cannot hold state) and supertype delegation generates the forwarding for you: the specification expands class C(delegatee: I) : I by delegatee into explicit overrides that call the delegate, and the docs call delegation 'a good alternative to implementation inheritance' that requires zero boilerplate. So the crossing protocol is declared as an interface, the platform end implements it as a real object, and the abstraction end implements it by delegating to the partner. The classic pair is still required when the second parent is a class with state (Thread, a framework base); the delegate expression is evaluated once at construction and may only use primary-constructor parameters, so the partner is passed in and the factory still links the two ends.
pitfalls: The delegate expression is evaluated once when the object is created and may not access the class's own properties or methods (only primary-constructor parameters), so the link can only be established after the first end exists - a factory or explicit link step is still needed.

Members overridden by the class are not called from the delegate's own implementations: when the delegate calls another method of the delegated interface, the delegate's version runs, not your override.
Delegation applies to interface supertypes only, so a second parent that is a class with state still requires the classic two-class pair.
On the JVM, interface members with bodies compile according to the -jvm-default mode, so binary compatibility with older Kotlin libraries can change which implementation is invoked.

variants.name: Classic twin pair (two classes with mutual references)
variants.idiom_name: two classes with mutual references (classic Twin, when the second parent is a stateful class)
variants.implementation_notes: When the second parent is a class that owns state - Thread, a framework base - Kotlin's delegation cannot help (it delegates interfaces only, and interfaces cannot hold state), so the realization is the classic pair: one class per parent, a partner property on each side, and a factory that links them. Keep the properties internal or private-set so the pair stays inside its module, and make the link explicit rather than derived from a constructor parameter so that both ends can be re-linked when one is replaced in a test.
pitfalls: lateinit moves the pair invariant to runtime: reading twin before the factory links it throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException instead of failing to compile.
Kotlin properties are public by default; declare the twin property internal or with a private setter so the partner does not become part of the module's API.
If either end also runs coroutines, the crossing calls must stay suspension-safe: a plain twin method call blocks the dispatcher thread the platform end runs on.
